1.  Parametric survival analysis in the **overall survival** framework.
2.  Parametric survival analysis in the **relative survival** framework.

## Lecture aims

1.  Describe the aims of survival analysis (overall survival).
2.  Describe parametric approaches to estimating the survival function.
3.  Describe two regression models: proportional hazards (PH) and accelerated failure time (AFT).
4.  Present software tools for survival analysis, with a real data example.
5.  Discuss other parametric, semiparametric and nonparametric alternatives.

# Survival analysis {background-color="#341B51"}

## Survival analysis in practice

-   In many areas, such as medicine, biology and engineering (reliability), scientists have access to the survival times of a group of individuals or items.
-   **Example 1.** The survival of cancer patients after a diagnosis of cancer.
-   **Example 2.** The lifespan of a product or device.
-   These two scenarios are identical from a theoretical perspective. In practice, however, the first one raises ethical considerations.

## The typical data set

-   A sample of **times to event**, possibly right-censored, $(t_1,\ldots,t_n)$, from a group of individuals.
-   The vital status (or **censoring indicators**) $(\delta_1,\ldots,\delta_n)$: $\delta_i=1$ for death, $\delta_i=0$ for right-censored (alive). Censoring may be due to random drop-out, loss to follow-up, or administrative censoring.
-   In some cases, we also know some characteristics of the individuals: **covariates** $\bx_i = (x_{i1},\ldots,x_{ip})^{\top}$, such as age, sex, deprivation level, comorbidities or tumour stage.
-   **Overall survival:** in this framework, we know the times to event, but we do not consider the cause of death.

## Censoring

![](figures/censor){fig-align="center" width="78%"}

## Aims of survival analysis

One of the aims of survival analysis is to quantify the survival of a group of individuals. The typical quantities of interest are:

1.  The **survival function**
    $$
    S(t) = 1- F(t) = \mathbb{P}(T>t),
    $$
    where $T$ is a positive random variable representing the survival time, with cdf $F$.
2.  The **hazard function**, defined as the instantaneous risk:
    $$
    h(t) = \lim_{\Delta t \to 0} \dfrac{\mathbb{P}(t \leq T < t+\Delta t \mid T \geq t)}{\Delta t} \exeq \dfrac{f(t)}{S(t)}.
    $$

## Survival and hazard functions

-   The hazard function and the survival function are linked through the relationship
    $$
    S(t) \exeq \exp\left\{ - \int_0^t h(s)\, ds \right\}.
    $$
-   The function $H(t) = \int_0^t h(s)\, ds$ is known as the **cumulative hazard function**.

## The importance of the hazard function

-   We are exposed to many forces of mortality: ageing, illnesses, natural disasters, accidents, crime, and so on.
-   In biostatistics (and epidemiology), the hazard plays a key role, as it reflects these forces of mortality.

# Parametric estimation without covariates {background-color="#341B51"}

## Maximum likelihood estimation: no covariates

-   Suppose that $(t_1,\ldots,t_n)$ are independent and identically distributed.
-   Suppose that we are interested in estimating the survival function using a parametric distribution $F(\cdot \mid \btheta)$.
-   Which distribution?

## A brief catalogue of parametric distributions

::: {.nonincremental}
-   [Gamma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gamma_distribution)
-   [Weibull](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weibull_distribution)
-   [Lognormal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Log-normal_distribution)
-   [Log-logistic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Log-logistic_distribution)
-   [Generalised gamma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generalized_gamma_distribution)
-   Among many others: [see this overview](https://rpubs.com/FJRubio/PGW).
:::

## Hazard shapes

Different distributions can capture different shapes of the hazard function:

-   **Weibull:** increasing, decreasing or constant.
-   **Lognormal:** unimodal (up, then down).
-   **Generalised gamma:** increasing, decreasing, bathtub or unimodal.

. . .

::: {.callout-important title="Warning" icon="false"}
By selecting a parametric distribution from the catalogue, we are making assumptions about the possible shapes of the true hazard function. Selecting the model using formal tools is usually recommended.
:::

## Maximum likelihood estimation: no covariates

-   We need to account for the different contributions of the $\obs{\text{observed}}$ and $\cens{\text{right-censored}}$ times:
    $$
    L(\btheta) = \prod_{i=1}^n \obs{f(t_i \mid \btheta)^{\delta_i}}\, \cens{S(t_i \mid \btheta)^{1-\delta_i}}.
    $$
-   The MLE $\widehat{\btheta}$ of $\btheta$ is the value that maximises the likelihood function (numerical methods are usually needed).
-   The fitted survival and hazard functions are $S(t\mid \widehat{\btheta})$ and $h(t\mid \widehat{\btheta})$.

## Software

-   Since these are standard methods and distributions, many have already been implemented in R.
-   For example, a number of distributions can be fitted to survival data using the [flexsurv](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/flexsurv/vignettes/flexsurv.pdf) R package.

# Regression models {background-color="#341B51"}

## Regression models: using covariates

-   Spoiler: there is no unique way of including covariates in a model for survival times.
-   Biostatisticians and epidemiologists tend to think in terms of the hazard, given the interpretation above. Unsurprisingly, most approaches to including covariates consist of **hazard-based regression models**.
-   The most popular are the **proportional hazards (PH)** model and the **accelerated failure time (AFT)** model.

## Proportional hazards models

-   The PH model postulates that the covariates act on a "baseline hazard", either increasing or decreasing it. That is,
    $$
    h_{\text{PH}}(t \mid \bx_i, \btheta,\bbeta) = h_0(t \mid \btheta) \exp\left\{ \bx_i ^{\top}\bbeta\right\}.
    $$
-   The corresponding cumulative hazard function is
    $$
    H_{\text{PH}}(t \mid \bx_i, \btheta,\bbeta) \exeq H_0(t \mid \btheta) \exp\left\{ \bx_i ^{\top}\bbeta\right\}.
    $$

## Proportional hazards: interpretation

-   $h_0(t \mid \btheta)$ is the hazard associated with $\bx_i = \mathbf{0}$, a sort of "reference point". It can be the hazard of any of the distributions discussed previously.
-   If $\bx_i ^{\top}\bbeta >0$, then $h_{\text{PH}}(t \mid \bx_i, \btheta,\bbeta) > h_0(t \mid \btheta)$: for a fixed value of $\bbeta$, the individual's combination of characteristics leads to an **increase** in the hazard compared with the baseline hazard.
-   If $\bx_i ^{\top}\bbeta <0$, then $h_{\text{PH}}(t \mid \bx_i, \btheta,\bbeta) < h_0(t \mid \btheta)$: the individual's combination of characteristics leads to a **decrease** in the hazard compared with the baseline hazard.

## Proportional hazards: hazard ratios

-   Let $\bx_i$ denote the characteristics of the $i$th patient and, for a specific $k\in\{1,\dots,p\}$, let $\tilde{\bx}_i$ be equal to $\bx_i$ except for its $k$th entry, $\tilde{x}_{ik} = x_{ik}+1$.
-   Then,
    $$
    \dfrac{h_{\text{PH}}(t \mid \tilde{\bx}_i, \btheta,\bbeta)}{h_{\text{PH}}(t \mid \bx_i, \btheta,\bbeta)} \exeq \exp\{\beta_k\}.
    $$
    That is, $\exp\{\beta_k\}$ is the **hazard ratio** associated with a one-unit increase in the covariate $x_{ik}$, with all other covariates held fixed.

## Accelerated failure time model

-   The AFT model postulates that the covariates act simultaneously on the time scale and on the hazard scale:
    $$
    h_{\text{AFT}}(t \mid \bx_i, \btheta,\bbeta) = h_0\left(t \exp\left\{ \bx_i ^{\top}\bbeta\right\}\mid \btheta\right) \exp\left\{ \bx_i ^{\top}\bbeta\right\}.
    $$
-   The corresponding cumulative hazard function is
    $$
    H_{\text{AFT}}(t \mid \bx_i, \btheta,\bbeta) \exeq H_0\left(t \exp\left\{ \bx_i ^{\top}\bbeta\right\}\mid \btheta\right).
    $$

## AFT model: interpretation

The interpretation of the AFT model is easier if we transform the model. The survival function is

$$
\begin{aligned}
S_{\text{AFT}}(t_i \mid \bx_i, \btheta,\bbeta) &\exeq \exp \left\{- H_0\left(t_i \exp\left\{ \bx_i ^{\top}\bbeta\right\}\mid \btheta\right) \right\} \\
&= S_0\left(t_i \exp\left\{ \bx_i ^{\top}\bbeta\right\}\mid \btheta\right)
= 1-F_0\left(t_i \exp\left\{ \bx_i ^{\top}\bbeta\right\}\mid \btheta\right)\\
&= \mathbb{P}\left( T_i > t_i \exp\left\{ \bx_i ^{\top}\bbeta\right\}\mid \btheta\right)
= \mathbb{P}\left(\log T_i > \log(t_i) + \bx_i ^{\top}\bbeta \mid \btheta\right)\\
&= \mathbb{P}\left(\log T_i > \log(t_i) - \bx_i ^{\top}\balpha \mid \btheta\right),
\end{aligned}
$$

where $\balpha = -\bbeta$.

## AFT model: interpretation (continued)

-   Let $Y_i = \log(T_i)$ and $Y_i - \bx_i^{\top}\balpha \sim G_0(\cdot \mid \btheta)$, with pdf $g_0$.
-   Then, writing $y_i = \log(t_i)$,
    $$
    \begin{aligned}
    S_{\text{AFT}}(t_i \mid \bx_i, \btheta,\bbeta) &\leftrightarrow 1-G_0\left( y_i - \bx_i ^{\top}\balpha \mid \btheta\right),\\
    f_{\text{AFT}}(t_i \mid \bx_i, \btheta,\bbeta) &\leftrightarrow g_0\left( y_i - \bx_i^{\top}\balpha \mid \btheta\right).
    \end{aligned}
    $$
-   We can identify this pdf with that of a **log-linear model**:
    $$
    y_i = \log(t_i) = \bx_i ^{\top}\balpha + \epsilon_i, \qquad \epsilon_i \stackrel{\text{iid}}{\sim} G_0(\cdot \mid \btheta), \quad i=1,\dots,n.
    $$
-   Consequently, the covariates have a direct effect on the log survival time.

## Regression models: the likelihood function

-   The likelihood function for the PH and AFT models is, for $j\in\{\text{PH},\text{AFT}\}$,
    $$
    \begin{aligned}
    L(\bbeta,\btheta) &= \prod_{i=1}^n \obs{f_{j}(t_i \mid \bx_i, \btheta,\bbeta)^{\delta_i}}\, \cens{S_{j}(t_i \mid \bx_i, \btheta,\bbeta)^{1-\delta_i}}\\
    &\exeq \prod_{i=1}^n h_{j}(t_i \mid \bx_i, \btheta,\bbeta)^{\delta_i} \exp\left\{ - H_{j}(t_i \mid \bx_i, \btheta,\bbeta) \right\}.
    \end{aligned}
    $$
-   This shows that the likelihood can be written entirely in terms of the hazard function.

# Example: lung cancer data {background-color="#341B51"}

## The data

-   Survival times $t_i$, $i=1,\dots,228$, of patients with advanced lung cancer from the North Central Cancer Treatment Group (available as `lung` in the R package **survival**).
-   165 patients died within the follow-up period (1,022 days).

## No covariates

-   We compare the survival functions of three parametric models: Weibull, lognormal and generalised gamma.
-   R code: [Example: no covariates](https://rpubs.com/FJRubio/PSM){.pill}

## Regression models

-   We consider two covariates, age and sex.
-   We first compare the PH and AFT models with a lognormal baseline hazard, and then with a Weibull baseline hazard (for which the PH and AFT models coincide).
-   R code: [Example: regression](https://rpubs.com/FJRubio/PSRM){.pill}

# Discussion {background-color="#341B51"}

## Discussion

-   Parametric survival models are useful tools in many applied areas.
-   Their use is not automatic: the user needs to select the parametric model(s).
-   PH and AFT models are the most popular hazard-based regression models.
-   Confidence intervals for the parameters, and confidence bands for the estimated survival function, can also be obtained.

## Extensions: parametric approaches

::: {.nonincremental}
-   The General Hazard (GH) model is an extension of the PH and AFT models.
-   The GH model is discussed in Lecture II.
-   The GH model is implemented in the R package [HazReg](https://github.com/FJRubio67/HazReg).
-   Other model structures include the proportional odds model and related extensions.
:::

## Extensions: semiparametric and nonparametric approaches

::: {.nonincremental}
-   The **Kaplan–Meier estimator** is a nonparametric estimator of the survival function.
-   The **Nelson–Aalen estimator** is a nonparametric estimator of the cumulative hazard function.
-   The **Cox model** is a semiparametric version of the PH model.
:::

R code: [Cox proportional hazards model](https://rpubs.com/FJRubio/CPHM){.pill}

## The Cox PH model and the partial likelihood

-   The PH model:
    $$
    h_{\text{PH}}(t\mid \bx_i, \bbeta) = h_0(t)\exp\left\{\bx_i^{\top}\bbeta \right\}.
    $$
-   To avoid misspecifying the baseline hazard, it is often preferred to leave it unspecified (estimating it nonparametrically), while the coefficients $\bbeta$ are estimated using the log partial likelihood function [@cox:1972]:
    $$
    \ell_p(\bbeta) = \sum_{i:\,\delta_i=1} \bx_i^{\top}\bbeta - \sum_{i:\,\delta_i=1} \log\left( \sum_{k \in \mathcal{R}(t_i)} \exp\left\{\bx_k^{\top}\bbeta\right\}\right),
    $$
    where $\mathcal{R}(t) = \{k : t_k \geq t\}$ denotes the risk set at time $t$.
